name: Offline-first sync to devices
summary: Keeping a copy of the data on each phone, browser or laptop, letting people read and write it with no connection, and merging the changes when they reconnect.
body: An offline-first app treats the copy on the device as the one it works with. Reads and writes go to a local database straight away, and a sync layer sends local changes to a server and pulls in everyone else’s when there is a network. The hard part is two devices changing the same record while apart. Systems answer that in different ways: Firestore’s offline cache lets the last write win; CouchDB keeps every conflicting revision, shows the same winner on every replica and leaves the losers for the application to merge; CRDT-based libraries merge most concurrent edits automatically.

When you compare systems, check what runs on the device (a full database, or a cache of recent queries), whether it syncs only the subset a user may see, how conflicts are detected and resolved, how long a device can stay offline, and whether the server side can be self-hosted or is tied to one cloud.
